html:
This label marks lands in Africa, and a patch of Europe, where people still lived by hunting, gathering and fishing around 3000 to 2000 BCE, while farming and herding spread around them.

It was the oldest human way of life. Small bands moved through the seasons, knew hundreds of plants and animals, used bows and small stone blades, and shared food widely. In southern and eastern Africa these were the ancestors of the Khoisan peoples and of foragers such as the Hadza. In the central African forests they were the ancestors of today's forest foragers.

The world around them was changing:

  • The end of the African Humid Period dried the green Sahara, pushing people toward the Nile and the Sahel.
  • Herders reached East Africa with cattle, sheep and goats around 3000 BCE.
  • Farmers in the Sahel took up pearl millet and sorghum.
  • In Europe farming had already reached almost everywhere; foragers held on mostly in the far north, like the taiga hunters.

Later the Bantu expansion carried farming and iron across most of Africa south of the equator, and foragers were absorbed or pushed into deserts and deep forest. On later maps they appear as savanna hunter-gatherers and similar labels.
sum: This label marks lands in Africa, and a patch of Europe, where people still lived by hunting, gathering and fishing around 3000 to 2000 BCE, while farming and herding spread around them.
